paras: The last two hundred kilometers were the hardest, and by the time I rolled into my own street, the bike and I were held together by tape and stubbornness. Three months on rough roads leave a mark. The next morning I dropped the bike off at the workshop and asked for a quote. The mechanic spun the wheels, listened to the bearings, and told me what I already knew: after that much wear and tear, a tune-up would not be enough. So I had the whole thing overhauled.

While the bike was in pieces, so was I. Everyone warns you about culture shock when you leave. Nobody warns you about reverse culture shock when you come back. The supermarket felt enormous. My own kitchen felt like somebody else's. There were four hundred emails waiting, a backlog that grew every hour, and I was swamped before I had even unpacked. So I did the small things first. I ran errands. I got the mail sorted, I had the water heater looked at, and I got my sister to drive me around for a week, until my own car was roadworthy again.

It took about a month to readjust, and what helped was not rushing it. I had my best photographs printed and put them on the wall, one for each country, and every evening I sat with them and let the trip settle. Friends kept asking when the next one was. The honest answer was: not yet. First I had to recharge my batteries, get the house back in order, and remember how to be a person who stays. The road will still be there. So, for that matter, will the bike, and this time it is in better shape than I am.
reading.source: Adapted from a long-distance cycling journal, The Long Way Home

gapfill.text: This text is full of the CAUSATIVE. You use it when somebody else does the work for you. THING: have / get + the THING + past participle. 'I HAD my bike OVERHAULED.' 'I GOT the mail SORTED.' PERSON: have + the PERSON + base form, or get + the PERSON + to + base form. 'I HAD the mechanic LOOK at it.' 'I GOT my sister TO DRIVE me.' The object always comes BEFORE the past participle: 'I had my bike serviced', never 'I had serviced my bike'.

bank.label: Useful language for getting things done
items: I had my bike completely overhauled before the trip.
I got the brakes checked at a shop in town.
I need to have the wheels looked at this week.
I am having the photographs printed on Friday.
I got my neighbor to water the plants while I was away.
I had the mechanic take a look at the gears.
I had my wallet stolen on the last day.
Where can I get this repaired around here?

lf.title: Which type? (blue = you asked a PERSON to do it)

lf.text: A and C are about a THING: have / get + the thing + past participle (serviced, checked). B and D, in blue, are about a PERSON: have + person + base form (had the mechanic LOOK), or get + person + to + base form (got my neighbor TO WATER). Ask yourself first: am I naming the job, or naming the person who does it?

items: Tell a friend three things you had done to your bike or your car before your last long trip. Use 'I had ...' plus a past participle.
You are away for a month. Say three things you got other people to do for you while you were gone.
Something went wrong abroad. Say what happened to you: 'I had my ... stolen / cancelled / delayed'.
You are back home and swamped. Say what you still need to get done this week, and who is going to do it.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = dropped the bike off, 2 = had the whole bike, 3 = got the mail, 4 = had the water heater, 5 = got his sister to, 6 = had his best photographs.
Model (a thing): 'I had my bike completely overhauled before the trip.'
Model (a person): 'I got my neighbor to water the plants while I was away.'
Structure: have / get + THING + past participle. Have + PERSON + base form. Get + PERSON + to + base form.
answerkey.note: Word order is everything. 'I had my bike serviced' means a mechanic did it. 'I had serviced my bike' means you did it yourself, earlier. And after 'get', a person needs 'to': 'I got my sister TO DRIVE me', never 'I got my sister drive me'.

listenings.text: Hi Marcelo, it is Kaia. You asked how bad my own homecoming was last year, so here is the honest list. I got back from Patagonia on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday I had already had the van towed, because of course it would not start after six weeks in a cold garage. Then I dropped my camera off at a shop in town, since the lens had taken a real beating, and the quote they gave me was almost the price of a new one. The wear and tear on my gear is always worse than the wear and tear on me. But the repairs were not the hard part. The office was. I had a backlog of two hundred emails and I was swamped for two solid weeks. In the end I got my brother to answer the easy ones while I dealt with the rest. So here is my advice. Do not try to readjust in a weekend. Give it a month, recharge your batteries, and have somebody else run your errands while you find your feet. Talk soon.

Welcome back to the show. Today, the part of the adventure that nobody puts in the photographs: coming home. Ask any long-distance traveler and you will hear the same thing. The trip ends, and then a second, much quieter trip begins. First there is the gear. Something always needs fixing, so you drop it off, you ask for a quote, and you discover that three months of wear and tear costs more than three months of flights. Then there is the house. You get the mail sorted, you have the water heater looked at, you get somebody to help you dig out from the backlog on your desk. And then there is you. Reverse culture shock is the strange, unglamorous truth of travel. The hardest border to cross is the one back into your own kitchen. So be patient with yourself. Give it a month. Recharge your batteries, get the small things done, and do not judge a journey by how quickly you readjust afterwards. The road changed you. Let home catch up.

extra_audio.text: First, the writer rides the last two hundred kilometers and reaches his own street with the bike barely holding together. Then, the next morning, he drops the bike off at the workshop and asks for a quote. After that, the mechanic tells him a tune-up is not enough, so he has the whole thing overhauled. Next, at home, he is swamped by a backlog of four hundred emails, so he gets the mail sorted and gets his sister to drive him around. Finally, he has his best photographs printed, hangs them on the wall, and gives himself a month to readjust.
